title: Folded surfaces such as villi and brain convolutions keep surface in step with mass

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Folded surfaces such as villi and brain convolutions keep surface in step with mass

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Throughout morphology, surface tends to keep pace with volume through changes of form, such as intestinal villi and folds, the shark's spiral valve, and brain convolutions whose complexity is correlated with animal size, so that a roughly constant ratio of surface to mass is maintained.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: S/M \approx \text{const} maintained by change of form, against S/M \propto L^{-1} for similar forms

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Throughout the whole field of morphology we may find examples of a tendency (referable doubtless in each case to some definite physical cause) for surface to keep pace with volume, through some alteration of its form.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Surface keeping pace with volume”. Scope: internal surfaces of animals, e.g. gut lining and brain cortex

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: S/M \approx \text{const} maintained by change of form, against S/M \propto L^{-1} for similar forms

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.53

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern 3D data permit tests for selected organs and taxa, and the scaling criterion is measurable. Existing datasets do not provide comparable surface and mass measurements across the broad morphological scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure internal surface area and body or organ mass across sizes for gut, spiral valve and cortex, then test whether folding maintains an approximately constant surface-to-mass ratio and whether fold complexity rises as predicted. Declining ratios despite folds or absent size-complexity associations would refute components.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Maintaining function rather than a constant geometric ratio is a plausible rival.

Different organs and taxa require incompatible imaging and segmentation.

Surface area is rarely annotated directly.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.35
discriminating power: 0.55
analysis feasibility: 0.5
data existence: 0.5

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: An invariant surface-to-mass ratio is a clear alternative to geometric scaling of a smooth surface, and brain images plus a few atlases make a start on cortex. They do not contain a cross-species surface-and-mass table, and intestinal villi and the shark spiral valve are even less centralized. The tendency throughout morphology can be probed for one or two organs only.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure surface area and mass for gut lining and cerebral cortex across body sizes. Surface per mass staying roughly constant, with folding or villi increasing with size, would support the claim; a smooth surface scaling as volume to the two-thirds would refute it for that organ.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Gut and brain surface areas are scattered by species and by measurement method.

Brain-image archives are dominated by a few model species rather than a body-size series.
